  to GNU Screen and first appeared in 2007. Nearly two decades later it remains one of the most widely used tools in the command line world, and for good
  reason. It solves a problem that anyone who works in a shell eventually runs into: a terminal is fragile, and the work running inside it depends on the window
  staying open.

  The core idea is simple. tmux runs as a server in the background, and each session it manages keeps its processes alive whether or not anyone is looking at
  them. You can start a long compile, a database migration, or a training run, detach from the session with a keystroke, close your laptop, and reattach hours
  later from the same machine or a different one over SSH. The shell never noticed you left. This turns a remote server from a place you have to babysit into a
  place you can simply visit.

  Within a session, tmux organizes work into windows, which behave like tabs, and panes, which split a window into several views side by side or stacked. A
  developer might keep an editor in one pane, a test runner in another, and a log tail in a third, all visible at once. Everything is driven from the keyboard.
  By default every command starts with a prefix key, Ctrl-b, followed by a letter, so splitting a pane or switching windows becomes muscle memory rather than a
  mouse gesture.

  tmux is also highly scriptable. Its configuration lives in a plain text file, usually ~/.tmux.conf, where users rebind keys, change colors, set mouse support,
  and adjust the status bar. Because every action is also available as a command, sessions can be created and arranged from shell scripts, which makes it
  practical to start a standard development layout with one command. Plugin managers have grown up around it, though many experienced users prefer a small,
  hand-written configuration.

  The tool does have a learning curve. Its vocabulary of sessions, windows, and panes takes a little time to internalize, and the default keybindings are not
  obvious. Scrollback and copy mode are unfamiliar to people raised on graphical terminals. Yet the investment pays off quickly, and the skills transfer
  everywhere, since tmux is available on nearly every Unix-like system.

  In the end, tmux rewards a simple habit: stop treating the terminal as disposable. Keep your work in sessions, detach when you leave, and reattach when you
  return. That small shift in workflow is what makes tmux indispensable.
